display_title: A novel unsupervised domain adaptation method

content.title: A novel unsupervised domain adaptation method
content.review:
This paper tackles the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). They present TFLG, a novel unsupervised domain adaptation method by extending the domain adversarial networks with a mini batch-wise feature GCN, and use it exploit the sample-level and class-level structure information. To transfer the relevant information from the source domain to target domain, TFLG uses the GCN features computed on the target domain, and the class-label relationship between the source domain and target domain to compute the features. The authors also propose memory-bank augmented TFLG to handle larger dataset where the class-label relationship becomes too sparse. 

Strengths

+ The paper is well written and well motivated.
+ Proposed method is a flexible module and can be plugged into existing UDA methods.

Weaknesses

- In Table 3, it would have been nice to know the performance of CDAN+TFLG with only cross-domain graph convolution
- Typo in Section 3.3: “In equation 8 ... across domains, b_nt” should have been “b_ns”. 
- In both Table1, table2, and section 4.2, it was not clear to me what “A->D” or “W->A” etc. stands for. It would have been nice to give a short description if they are dataset specific.
- My main concern is in the experiments section, according to table 2 the improvements over CDANE is not significant in larger datasets such as Office-Home, and this makes me wonder how it would perform on larger datasets such as LVIS which is closer to practical settings.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Review #3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.
1. We evaluate the performance of CDAN+TFLG with only cross-domain graph convolution on Office-31. In this experiment, we only use the GCN features as input for domain discriminator and image classifier. The results are as follows:

A->W: 81.2    D->W: 95.7   W->D: 97.6   A->D: 85.9   D->A: 63.2   W->A: 63.1   Avg: 81.1

 Compared with the average accuracy of only using CNN features, which is 87.1,  there is a 6% difference between them. This phenomenon is not surprising. Because GCN learns the entity representation by propagating neighbor information while CNN focuses on extracting features from the entity itself.

2. Thank you for pointing out the typo. We have revised it.

3. Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We will add a short description in paper. Taking A->D as an example, A (Amazon) is the source dataset and D (DSLR) is the target dataset.

3. We evaluate our proposed method on the VisDA2017 dataset, which is a large-scale dataset with 12 classes and more than 280k images. It includes two very different domains: the Synthetic (source domain), which is generated by 3D models from different angles and lightning conditions; the Real (target domain), which consists of natural images. In this dataset, CDAN obtains an accuracy of 66.8%, while our method CDAN+TFLGM obtains 68.8%.

display_title: An intuitive idea but lacking originality and experimental comparisons

content.title: An intuitive idea but lacking originality and experimental comparisons
content.review:
This paper introduces an approach to account for the structure of the data for unsupervised domain adaptation. In essence, structure-aware features are extracted via a graph convolutional network acting on a graph whose node represent the different samples in a mini-batch. The structure-aware features extracted from a source mini-batch are then combined with those from a target mini-batch according to the class (pseudo-)labels of the samples.

Strengths:
- Taking the structure of the data into account when performing domain adaptation seems intuitive, and so does using a GCN to encode this structure.
- The paper is reasonably clearly written, and the methodology should be reproducible with some effort
- The experiments evaluate different aspects of the proposed method


Weaknesses:

Originality:
- While I find the idea of modeling the data structure during the domain adaptation process attractive, this paper is not the first one to propose a solution that does so. In particular, as very briefly discussed by the authors in the related work section, Ma et al., 2019 also introduced a solution to doing so with GCN acting on the source and target mini-batches. I acknowledge that the specifics of the two solutions differ, but this seriously limits the originality of this submission.

Related work:
- As stated above, the discussion of Ma et al., 2019 is very brief. Considering the similarities between both methods, I suggest the author to provide a much more detailed explanation of this work and of the differences with the proposed method.
- To a lesser degree Ding et al., 2018 should also be discussed in more detail, as it also relies on the notion of graph structure of the data, albeit for label propagation.

Methodology:
- In the introduction (top of page 2), the authors mention that a domain discriminator might struggle when the discrepancy between the source and target domains is large. While I agree with this, I do not see how the proposed method tackles this issue.
- I do not understand the intuition behind the formulation in Eq. 8. This essentially adds features extracted from the source samples to those of the target samples. The value of these features will depend on what samples are seen in the mini-batch. I would highly appreciate if the authors could justify this design choice.

Experiments:
- A comparison to the most important baseline (Ma et al., 2019) is missing. This is the closest work to the proposed method, which essentially only differs from it in the way it uses the GCN features. For this paper to be valuable, it needs to show that the proposed method is a better way to encode the data structure, and ideally to provide an explanation why. Note that the numbers reported in (Ma et al, 2019), while on the same dataset, were obtained with a different backbone architecture (AlexNet vs ResNet-50). Therefore, one cannot directly compare these numbers.
- The results on ImageCLEF in the appendix are less convincing than on the other datasets. Do the authors have an explanation why?

Minor comments/questions:
- The minimization problems in Eq 3 should also depend on the feature extractor G.
- At the end of the intro, extensive experiments are not a contribution per se.
- Is TFLG(w/o cg) equivalent to setting \gamma to 0, or does it represent something else?
- Considering that the results of t-SNE depend on initialization, I am not confident that one can draw conclusions from Figure 5 in the appendix, where the t-SNE results for CDAN and CDAN+TFLG are quite similar.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

replying_to: Replying to An intuitive idea but lacking originality and experimental comparisons

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.

In response to originality and relate work:

GCAN[1] (Ma et al, 2019) is an end-to-end Graph Convolutional Adversarial Network (GCAN) for unsupervised domain adaptation by jointly modeling data structure, domain label and class label in a unified deep model. GCN is applied to model data structure. Firstly, they use the Data Structure Analyzer (DSA) network to learn CNN features for mini-batch samples and utilize the learned features to construct a dense-connected instance graph based on the similarity of pairwise mini-batch samples. Secondly, they apply the Graph Convolution Network (GCN) on the instance graph to learn GCN features. Finally, they concatenate CNN (a CNN network different from DSA) and GCN features as the input for domain alignment and class centroid alignment modules. The major differences between our method and GCAN are as follow: 
1. Our method does not require a specific CNN network, e.g., DSA, to build the dense-connected instance mini-graph. Instead, we use the same CNN network to build mini-graph and extract CNN features. 
2. GCAN directly uses the GCN to extract features for target samples, while we proposed the cross-domain graph convolutional operation to explore class-level and sample-level structure information by bridging the source and the target domains. Our ablation studies also demonstrate the importance of the cross-domain graph convolutional operation. 
3. To better capture the class-level relationship and transfer relevant data-structural information across the source and target domains, we maintain a memory bank for source domain to store the most recent batches of source GCN features, which has been proved to be effective.
4.  Our proposed cross-domain graph convolutional operation can be easily integrated with various adversarial learning based unsupervised domain adaptation approaches, such as DANN, CDAN and CDANE.

GAKT [2] (Ding et al., 2018) is a Graph Adaptive Knowledge Transfer (GAKT) model that jointly optimizes target labels and domain-free features in a unified framework, which doesn’t involve graph convolutional operations or adversarial learning. GAKT is not considered as a baseline as it adopts a very different technical approach and the performance is not comparable with the adversarial learning based methods.

We have added detailed discussions on the related methods GCAN and GAKT in the final version.

[1] CVPR2019: GCAN: Graph Convolutional Adversarial Network for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation.

[2] ECCV2018: Graph Adaptive Knowledge Transfer for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation.

In response to methodology:
1. About large domain discrepancy. It is possible that a large domain gap may make domain discriminator not easy to be deceived. In our proposed cross-domain graph convolutional operation, we bridge the source and the target domains by adding the source structure information into target structure, which helps gradually merge the source and target domains, and increase the difficulty for domain discriminator to correctly distinguish two domains. The results on Office-Home prove the efficacy of the proposed cross-domain graph convolutional operation for transfer tasks with large domain gap. For instance, our method can significantly improve the performances on several hard tasks, e.g., Ar->Cl, Cl->Ar and Pr->Ar, compared with the baseline CDAN.
2. About the intuition behind the Eq. 8. The goal of Eq. 8. is to attentively distill relevant sample-level and class-level structure information from source graph to target graph. First, we build mini-graph for source batch samples and extract their sample-level structure information Z_s. Second, we build the transfer matrix T (in Eq. 8) by source labels and target pseudo-labels, which represents the class label relationship between source and target domain. Finally, in Eq. 8, the second item \gamma\sigma(TZ_sW_{tra}), where W_{tra} is the parameter of transfer layer, can introduce sample-level and class-level structure information from source domain to target domain. The Eq. 8 connects and propagates the target graph knowledge and source graph information by graph reasoning.

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
In response to experiments:
1. About the comparison with GCAN. We cannot directly compare with the reported results in the GCAN paper, due to the different backbone architectures. In fact, we have contacted the authors of GCAN paper to request the source codes, but did not get any response. We have also tried to reimplement the GCAN method by following the implementation details in the paper, however, we could not obtain meaningful results. We will report the detailed results of GCAN, including both the original results with AlexNet backbone and the results from our reimplementation with ResNet-50 backbone, in the final version.
2. About the results on ImageCLEF. For Office-31, compared with CDAN, CDAN+TFLG boosts the accuracy by 2% on average. For Office-Home, CDAN+TFLGM has a 2.1% advantage over CDAN. For ImageCLEF-DA, CDAN+TFLG outperforms CDAN with up to 1.6% on average accuracy. We understand the concern in ImageCLEF-DA results that the performance improvement is not as significant as in Office-31 and Office-Home. In fact, we still observe the benefit of the cross-domain graph convolutional operation on hard transfer tasks, e.g., I->P and C->P, where our method boosts the accuracy by 2.4% and 2.5% compared with baseline. It still proves the efficacy of our proposed method.

In response to minor comments/questions:
1. Thank you for pointing out the problems. We have revised it.
2. Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have revised section 1 accordingly.
3. Yes. TFLG(w/o cg) is equal to setting \gamma to 0 in Eq. 8.
4. In fact, we can see the features learned by CDAN have more scattered target features (red dots), which are not close to the source features (blue dots), than CDAN+TFLG.

display_title: Marginal novelty with UDA settings of less interest

content.title: Marginal novelty with UDA settings of less interest
content.review:
The authors proposed a transferable graph-based feature learning scheme, which can be applied to address the task of unsupervised domain adaptation. With both sample and class-level structural information exploited, improved performances were reported. Generally, the paper is clearly written and easy to follow. My review comments are discussed below.

I found the paper to be technically sound but with marginal novelty. Based on DANN-like architecture (i.e., use of adversarial learning for domain adaptation), the authors proposed additional GCN layers to process the features, while additionally adaptation performed by regularization on local structure of the same label (i.e., T*Z_s*W_tra).  Adding/observing such local and class-level structural consistency has been observed in existing vision and learning models, and this is the reason why I feel the novelty would be marginal.

After such an additional GCN-based feature extraction stage, the derived feature is concatenated with the original ResNet features (w/o adaptation) for final domain adaptation. On the datasets like Office-31/home, one would expect ResNet-like deep features are robust enough to describe such cross-domain data. Thus, adding extra GCN-based features (which require additional parameters for feature learning) for producing slightly improved results would not be very surprising. I'm not saying that the experiment results always need to show a clear margin when comparing to others, but I feel that such improvements were simply due to extra efforts on feature learning and thus can be expected.

Lastly, UDA settings considered in this paper have been well studied over the past decade. Recently, researchers shift their interests to more advanced/challenging settings like partial DA [A], universal DA [B], etc. This is also the reason why I feel that this paper might not be of sufficient interest to the community.

[A] Cao et al., Partial domain adaptaion, ECCV 2018
[B] You et al., Universal domain adaptation, CVPR 2019
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Response to Review #4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.
1. We would like to clarify the major contribution of our work as follows. We design a graph convolution operator that exploits class-level and sample-level structure across two domains and helps improve the performance of adversarial unsupervised domain adaptation methods, e.g., DANN, CDAN and CDANE. In our ablation study, we further prove the efficacy of the proposed graph convolution operator which includes mini-graph convolution and cross-domain graph convolutional operation. In comparison, the baselines include DANN, CDAN, DANN+mini-graph convolution, and CDAN+mini-graph convolution. As mentioned by the reviewer, adding extra GCN-based features, e.g., DANN+mini-graph convolution and CDAN+mini-graph convolution, will slightly improved results, which is validated by comparing the results of DANN/CDAN and those of DANN/CDAN+mini-graph convolution. Moreover, we further introduce the cross-domain graph convolutional operation to explore class-level and sample-level structure information by bridging source and target domains. The results of DANN+TFLG and CDAN+TFLG prove the importance of cross-domain graph convolutional operation by comparing with DANN/CDAN+mini-graph convolution.
2. We appreciate the suggestions for the new direction. We will explore how to apply our proposed method to solve the new problems and consider them as our future work.

display_title: Intuitive extension with the help of graph network

content.title: Intuitive extension with the help of graph network
content.review:
# Summary

In this paper, the authors propose a graph network module to capture the sample-level and class-level structure for unsupervised domain adaptation. Compared to the existing UDA methods, which focus on adversarial domain-invariant feature learning, the proposed system augments the representation learning part with the recent practice of graph network. The main motivation is that both source and target domains share the same label space so that such structured knowledge could be crucial to bridge the gap between source and target domains. The extensive empirical studies on several domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The overall writing looks good to me. The storyline is consistent and well-motivated. The authors provide enough detail to shed light on the design choices for the state-of-the-art UDA approach. The figures and tables are also quite informative. For example, I particularly love the figure 1 because it helps the readers catch up with the overall architecture of the proposed system.

# Questions

1. Even though the source and target domains share the same label space, the actual semantic prior could be different. For example, let's think of the real-world long-tailed distributed data. Both source (evenly sampled) and target (long-tail) could have the same label space, but the label priors are quite different. It could be much more helpful if the authors could also discuss this situation.

2. The proposed TFLG and TFLGM approaches utilize the pseudo label. I noticed that all these domain adaptation experiments have a strong baseline to start with. For example, most of the classification accuracies on office-31 are above 60%. I wonder if the proposed module could still be helpful when the initial guess on target data is too bad to be trusted with.

3. Considering the potential of the real-world application, I am suggesting that the authors could also include the additional computational cost of the proposed module. The extra graph network looks expensive to me, especially the memory bank version. It could be helpful to also discuss this perspective as well.

---- Post-rebuttal comments----

I agree with the other reviewers' concerns so that I turn down my rating.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Review #2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments.
1. Thank you for offering this very good insight. In fact, the traditional unsupervised domain adaptation methods, especially the adversarial learning based ones, prefer to globally merge two domains without considering this problem. In our method, we build graphs for source and target domains to exploit their structure information. Specifically, in our proposed cross-domain graph convolutional operation, we bridge the source and target domains to explore their class-level and sample-level structure information by using transfer matrix T, which is built by the relationship between source labels and target pseudo-labels. Therefore, our method can find reliable correspondence between source and target domains even when their semantic priors are different. We will add more detailed discussions in the final version. 
2. With regard to bad initialization on target data, e.g., the classification accuracies on target data are below 50%. We can look into some transfer tasks on the Office-Home dataset, e.g., Ar->Cl. The accuracy of CDAN for this task is 49%, while our TFLGM method improves the accuracy to 50.7%, which proves the efficacy of our proposed method under bad initialization.
3. For the sake of fair comparison, we set the same batch size 36 for CDAN, CDAN+TFLG and CDAN+TFLGM (memory bank size is 36*4).  CDAN occupies 7513MiB GPU memory and takes 0.2975s for each iteration, CDAN+TFLG uses 7983MiB GPU memory and needs 0.3685s for one iteration, and CDAN+TFLGM uses 7985MiB GPU memory and takes 0.4559s for one iteration.
